question.text: A bank's treasury desk expects the yield curve to steepen, with the 10-year GOI yield rising relative to the 6-year GOI yield. Using GOI bond futures, which inter-bond spread (steepener) trade implements this view?

answer.text: Buy 6-year GOI bond futures and sell 10-year GOI bond futures
Sell both 6-year and 10-year GOI bond futures
Buy both 6-year and 10-year GOI bond futures
Buy 10-year and sell 6-year GOI bond futures (flattener)

explanation.text: The Logic: If the 10-year yield rises relative to the 6-year yield (curve steepening), then because bond prices move inversely to yields, the 10-year futures price falls relative to the 6-year futures price. A steepener that profits from this is long 6-year futures and short 10-year futures (option A). NISM Series IV pp.160-161 describes inter-bond spread strategies as long-short positions in futures on different GOI bonds keyed to steepening or flattening views. The Trap: Option B is a directional short, not a spread. Option C is a directional long. Option D is the flattener trade - the opposite of what the steepening view requires. In the original ambiguous version the stem said the "spread between futures" had narrowed and would widen, without specifying whether "spread" meant price spread or yield spread. Because price spread and yield spread move in opposite directions, the keyed buy-6Y/sell-10Y trade depended on an unstated convention. Note: The original question was ambiguous because "spread" between two bond futures can mean price spread or yield spread, and the two conventions give opposite trades. The stem has been rewritten as a yield-curve steepening view with the 10-year yield rising relative to the 6-year yield, so option A is uniquely correct. Source: NISM Series IV, Dec 2025, pp.160-161, 190.
